steps.body:
Differentiation drops the exponent in front and lowers the power. So **run it backwards**: raise the power, then divide by the new power.

∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.

And check by differentiating. It takes ten seconds and catches nearly every error.

explanationVariants: An antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Differentiate it back: (x⁴/4)′ = 4x³/4 = x³ ✓.
Raise 3 to 4, then divide by the new power, 4. The division is what undoes the coefficient the power rule would have produced.

options.label: x⁴/4 + C
options.feedback: Right — and differentiating it back gives 4x³/4 = x³, which is the only check you ever need.

options.label: 3x² + C
options.feedback: That is the DERIVATIVE of x³. Integration runs the other way: raise the power, do not lower it.

options.label: x⁴ + C
options.feedback: Differentiate it back: (x⁴)′ = 4x³, which is four times too big. You must divide by the new power.

options.label: x⁴/3 + C
options.feedback: You divided by the OLD power. Divide by the new one: 4.

steps.body: The same area, computed the fast way.

widget.prompt: Squeeze the rectangles toward the area under x² on [0, 2]. The antiderivative says it is exactly 8/3.
widget.successFeedback: The rectangles are converging on 2.667, and F(x) = x³/3 gave that in one line: 8/3 − 0. Every Riemann sum in this course was grinding toward a number that a single antiderivative hands you instantly. That is the trade the Fundamental Theorem makes.
widget.lowFeedback: Still short of 8/3 ≈ 2.667. Raise n, or switch rule.
widget.highFeedback: Still above 8/3. Raise n, or come down from the right rule.

cml.actionGoal: Partition an interval and compare how sample rules accumulate approximate signed area.

explanationVariants: Antidifferentiate each term: 3x² → x³, and 2x → x². So F(x) = x³ + x², and ∫₁² = (8 + 4) − (1 + 1) = 10.
Sums split for antiderivatives exactly as they do for derivatives — the linearity runs both ways.

commonErrors.feedback: That is F(2) = 8 + 4 = 12 — you forgot to subtract F(1) = 2.
Check F: an antiderivative of 3x² is x³ (not 3x³/3 × 3), and of 2x is x². F(2) − F(1) = 12 − 2 = 10.
That is F(1). The answer is F(2) − F(1) = 12 − 2 = 10.

steps.body:
Why the **+ C**?

Because a constant has zero slope, x⁴/4 and x⁴/4 + 7 have the *same* derivative. Antidifferentiating cannot recover information the derivative destroyed.

So an indefinite integral is a whole **family** of parallel curves. For a definite integral, C cancels in the subtraction and you may ignore it.

explanationVariants: For ∫ₐᵇ f the constant cancels: [F(b) + C] − [F(a) + C] = F(b) − F(a). For an indefinite integral it does not, because there is nothing to subtract it against.
The derivative threw away the constant; only extra information — like a starting value — can put it back.

widget.prompt: When does the + C actually matter?

options.label: For indefinite integrals — a definite integral subtracts it away.
options.feedback: Right. The subtraction F(b) − F(a) annihilates C, which is why nobody writes it when evaluating a definite integral.

options.label: Never — it is a formality.
options.feedback: It is not. ∫ 2x dx is the whole family x² + C, and the curves through (1, 5) and (1, 0) are genuinely different functions.

options.label: Always, including for definite integrals.
options.feedback: In a definite integral C appears in both F(b) and F(a) and cancels exactly. Carrying it is harmless but pointless.

options.label: Only when the constant is large.
options.feedback: Size is irrelevant. What matters is whether there is a subtraction to cancel it.

hints: There is no quotient rule for integrals, and you do not need one. Simplify first.
Now antidifferentiate term by term: x³/3 + x. Evaluate from 1 to 3.
explanationVariants: Simplify to x² + 1, whose antiderivative is x³/3 + x. Then F(3) − F(1) = (9 + 3) − (1/3 + 1) = 12 − 4/3 = 32/3 ≈ 10.667.
Integration has far fewer rules than differentiation, which is why rewriting first is not a convenience — it is often the only way through.

widget.prompt: ∫₁³ (x³ + x)/x dx (for x ≠ 0). Give a decimal to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12 — you forgot to subtract F(1) = 4/3 ≈ 1.333.
Check the simplification: (x³ + x)/x = x² + 1, not x³ + 1. The x cancels one power.
That is F(1). The answer is F(3) − F(1) = 12 − 1.333 = 10.667.

steps.body: Raise the power, divide by the new one.
takeaways: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1. Always check by differentiating back.
The + C is a whole family of parallel curves — the derivative destroyed that information and antidifferentiation cannot invent it.
In a definite integral C cancels, so ignore it. In an indefinite one it is part of the answer.
steps.teaser: Next: one extra fact pins C down — and turns a family into a single curve.

concept.body: Two moves, and then a check. **Raise** the exponent by one. **Divide** by the new exponent. Then **differentiate your answer** — if it does not give back what you started with, you have made an error and you will know instantly.

explanationVariants: An antiderivative of x⁴ is x⁵/5, since (x⁵/5)′ = 5x⁴/5 = x⁴.

options.label: x⁵/5 + C
options.feedback: Right — differentiate it back and the 5s cancel, leaving x⁴.

options.label: 4x³ + C
options.feedback: That is the derivative. Integration raises the power rather than lowering it.
